source.title: Summer-22B: A Systematic Approach to Dataset Engineering and Training at Scale for Video Foundation Model

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites language-model scaling work but does not test or rely on the claim’s loss-scaling laws. Its reported scaling experiments concern learning-rate transfer, not loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.gate_note: The paper reports µP learning-rate transfer across model sizes and training durations, but not loss power-law fits or predictions. It also reports architecture comparisons using validation CLIP similarity rather than the held-out loss named in V4; this related result is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: This is a video-diffusion technical report. It cites Chinchilla only in related work and fits no loss law in parameters, tokens or compute. Its 'scaling laws' are empirical learning-rate rules (LR ∝ √B, LR ∝ 1/√T) and µP transfer, a different construct. Its architecture ablation compares attention variants of video DiTs by validation CLIP similarity, with no numbers. It does not vary depth or width and does not use the held-out language-model loss that V4 names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that dataset engineering dominated the effort and that monitoring parameter dynamics within the 'µP band' caught instabilities. They report VBench 2.0 total 0.539 vs Wan 2.2-5B 0.575, at about $300K total cost. The architecture claim is stated as holding 'up to 1B parameters, 100K steps', although the ablation itself was run at 100M parameters and 10K steps.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not measure the original loss-scaling laws. Its scale experiments test µP learning-rate transfer and empirical learning-rate relationships with batch size and training duration.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors caution that their learning-rate scaling observations may not generalize beyond their video-diffusion architecture and data. Architecture results are limited to 100M parameters and 10K steps.

fits_no_version.finding: At 100M parameters and 10K steps, five attention-architecture variants reached similar validation CLIP similarity, with differences smaller than run-to-run variance. Differential Attention became unstable at billion-parameter scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In video diffusion transformers, attention-mechanism variants change validation CLIP similarity little at small scale, but some become unstable at larger scale.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal learning rate scaled roughly as √B and as 1/√T. µP transferred learning rates from 30M to 1B parameters and from 1K to 100K steps, under hypersphere constraints. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate follows simple power rules in batch size and training duration under µP with hypersphere-constrained optimization.

record.problems: No experiments fit or evaluate held-out-loss power laws against parameter count, tokens, or compute. The architecture comparison reports CLIP similarity rather than held-out loss and is limited to 100M parameters and 10K steps.

untested.parts: All: no loss power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation of loss from small to large runs.
Effect of depth, width and shape on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling for video diffusion is not fitted, even though models of 30M–1B parameters were trained.
No relation between scale or loss and VBench scores is reported.
No exponents or allocations are compared across setups.

record.verdict_notes: The µP sweeps recorded final validation loss across 30M/100M/1B parameters and 1K/10K/100K steps. These could in principle bear on V1/V5, but no loss values or fits are reported, so nothing can be extracted.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in video or other modalities and training regimes.
Downstream-task performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: five distinct architectural variants
rows.operation_detail: Compared architecture variants’ validation CLIP similarity during training.

conditions.value: standard transformer with 3D RoPE, Multi-Latent Attention, window attention, different local attention patterns, and differential attention

rows.measure: Validation CLIP similarity; the text says the variants achieved similar final performance and their differences were smaller than run-to-run variance.
rows.value: Similar final performance; overlapping trajectories are described for the Cross-attention DiT and Simple DiT comparison.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the five variants; the figure specifically compares Cross-attention DiT and Simple DiT. This is a CLIP-similarity/performance result, not a held-out-loss result.
rows.check: Not linked to V4: the subject is attention-mechanism variants of video diffusion transformers, not depth or width of language models. The measure is validation CLIP similarity, not held-out loss, and no numeric values or baseline are given. The 'observed' state has no version to be checked against. Figure 15 compares Cross-attention DiT with Simple DiT, which is not the same set as the five Section 5.1 variants.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
